name: Bambu Cool Plate SuperTack (proprietary low-temp coating on spring steel)
summary: Bambu Lab's low-temperature adhesion plate: a ~0.05 mm proprietary 'SuperTack' polymer coating on a 0.4 mm spring-steel base, engineered to grip PLA hard at 35-45 degC bed temperatures instead of the 60 degC-plus a PEI sheet wants. It is not PEI and behaves nothing like one — adhesion is chemical tack rather than thermal-expansion mismatch, the coating is soft and scratch-prone, and materials outside the PLA/PETG envelope (notably TPU) are documented to damage it.
surface_makeup: Undisclosed proprietary polymer coating approximately 0.05 mm thick, applied to a 0.4 mm spring-steel base sheet; Bambu describes it only as a 'specially designed coating' and does not publish the chemistry. Explicitly not polyetherimide, and distinct from the older bare polycarbonate Cool Plate it replaced. Single-sided (one coated face).

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: The plate's entire reason to exist. Full adhesion at bed temperatures well below what PEI needs, which cuts warp on large flat parts and keeps the chamber cool. Parts normally pop free unaided once the bed drops to room temperature.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: As base PLA; toughened blends make no measurable difference to release behaviour.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: As base PLA, with a glossy bottom face since the coating is smooth rather than powder-textured.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: High-flow PLA is the material this plate is marketed alongside on the A1/P1/X1 high-speed profiles; behaviour matches base PLA.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: glue stick as a release barrier if attempted
filament_compatibility.notes: Bambu's own wiki warns that its PLA Silk bonds so hard to SuperTack that removal may damage the printed model. Third-party silk PLAs vary but should be treated the same until tested on a scrap part.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: Not called out in Bambu's compatibility list. Adhesion follows base PLA, but stiff CF-filled parts do not flex with the sheet, so they lever against a soft coating during removal — flex from the far edge and expect scratching.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none on the part; PETG supports must never touch the plate
filament_compatibility.notes: Officially supported and Bambu publishes a dedicated PETG-on-SuperTack guide, but this is the plate's most contested material: multiple forum threads report over-adhesion, torn coating and poor first layers. Bambu Studio blocks slicing when PETG support material would contact the first layer because it will damage the plate.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: Treat exactly as PETG, including the rule that no copolyester support may print directly on the coating.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: As PETG; unmodified PET is not separately characterised by Bambu on this plate.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: Fibre fill lowers peak bond strength slightly versus neat PETG, but the rigid part still risks lifting coating on removal.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none
filament_compatibility.notes: Not on Bambu's supported list (unverified). Bed temperature is within the plate's envelope and adhesion is generally good, but do not use IPA to help release — it dissolves PVB and the plate's own cleaning guidance is water and detergent anyway.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: use a textured or engineering PEI plate instead
filament_compatibility.notes: Absent from the supported material list and well above the plate's low-temperature design point. Bambu directs styrenics to the Engineering, High-Temp or Textured PEI plates.

preparation: No seasoning or break-in is needed on first use; wash the factory coating with warm water and a mild detergent, dry it fully, and mount it coated-side up (it is single-sided). Routine prep is the same wash whenever first-layer adhesion softens — do not reach for solvents. The step people skip is Bambu's own instruction to wipe the nozzle repeatedly in the plate's dedicated wiping zone before every print and before auto-levelling, so that a bead of cooled filament on the nozzle tip does not corrupt the bed-mesh probe or drag through the fresh first layer. Because the coating grips at 35-45 degC, resist the habit of raising bed temperature to fix a bad first layer; on SuperTack a too-hot bed makes over-adhesion worse, not better, and first-layer problems are almost always Z-offset or a dirty nozzle instead.
cleaning: Wash with water and a mild detergent or dish soap, using a soft cloth or sponge, then dry completely before remounting so nothing is trapped against the steel. That is the whole officially sanctioned procedure. Explicitly avoid organic solvents — acetone in particular is called out as damaging to the coating, and there is no evidence the coating tolerates the routine IPA wipe that PEI users take for granted, so treat alcohol as a last resort rather than the default. Never use abrasive pads, scouring powder, wire brushes or blades: the tack layer is only about 0.05 mm thick and anything that abrades it removes adhesion permanently in that spot. Baked-on filament from a nozzle crash should be softened by warming the bed to that material's print bed temperature and lifted with a plastic tool, never chiselled cold.
model_removal: Let the bed cool fully to room temperature and most PLA prints release on their own or with a light flex of the sheet off the magnet — that is the intended workflow and the one that preserves the coating. Do not remove parts while the bed is warm: SuperTack's bond is strongest hot, which is the opposite intuition from PEI users who pry ABS off warm. When a part still holds, use the supplied plastic scraper at a shallow angle from a corner rather than levering from above. Bambu acknowledges the coating is comparatively soft and that scraper scratches are cosmetic and do not affect function, but every scratch is a place where future first layers behave differently, so minimise them. Rigid parts with large flat footprints — CF-filled PLA especially — should be released by flexing the sheet progressively from one edge instead of trying to pop the whole footprint at once.
stuck_print_recovery: Bambu's official first move is counter-intuitive but effective: reheat the bed to roughly 50 degC, which softens the tack layer enough to let a stubborn part shear off, then lift it immediately. If that fails, the generic toolkit applies with caveats — freezer cooling for 10-15 minutes exploits the steel/polymer contraction mismatch and works, and unwaxed dental floss or thin wire sawed under the footprint is the safest mechanical option because it applies shear rather than a point load. IPA wicking under the perimeter is the technique to be most careful with here, since alcohol is outside the vendor's sanctioned cleaning regime for this coating; if you use it, keep it at the part edge and wash the plate afterwards. Whatever you do, do not escalate to a metal blade or heavy prying — on a 0.05 mm coating that trades a stuck print for a permanently dead patch of plate. Over-adhered PETG and Bambu PLA Silk are the two cases most likely to reach this point, and both are better prevented than recovered.

damage_avoidance.reason: Bambu calls acetone out specifically as damaging to the coating. The chemistry is undisclosed and roughly 0.05 mm thick, so there is no margin and no way to reason about what a given solvent will do; the only officially sanctioned cleaning agent is water with a mild detergent.

damage_avoidance.item: Isopropyl alcohol as a routine wipe
damage_avoidance.reason: The habit every PEI owner brings to this plate and the one Bambu's documentation does not support. Water and mild detergent is the entire sanctioned procedure, and there is no published evidence the coating tolerates repeated alcohol. Treat IPA as a last resort confined to the edge of a stuck part, and wash the plate afterwards rather than adopting it as the pre-print routine.

damage_avoidance.item: Abrasive pads, scouring powder, wire brushes and sandpaper
damage_avoidance.reason: The exact opposite of the PEI rule. On powder-coated or laminated PEI, a light uniform abrasive pass is a documented way to expose fresh material and restore grip; on a 0.05 mm tack layer with nothing equivalent underneath, anything abrasive removes adhesion permanently in that spot and there is no restoration path or recoating service.

On a coating this thin, forcing a stuck print with steel trades one print for a permanently dead patch of plate. Bambu supplies a plastic scraper and expects it to enter at a shallow angle from a corner; floss or thin wire drawn under the footprint is safer still because it applies shear rather than a point load.

damage_avoidance.item: Removing parts at full bed temperature
damage_avoidance.reason: SuperTack's bond is strongest hot, which inverts the intuition of PEI users accustomed to lifting ABS warm. Note the careful distinction from Bambu's own recovery advice: a deliberate reheat to roughly 50 degC softens the tack layer enough to shear a stubborn part off and is sanctioned, but pulling at a plate still at printing temperature is not.

damage_avoidance.item: Raising bed temperature to rescue a first layer, or exceeding roughly 70 degC
damage_avoidance.reason: The coating grips at 35-45 degC, and on this plate a hotter bed makes over-adhesion worse rather than better, so the reflex fix makes the problem it was meant to solve. First-layer trouble here is almost always Z-offset or a dirty nozzle. No maximum surface temperature is published, so the ceiling in this entry is inferred from the supported PLA and PETG envelope.

damage_avoidance.item: Over-adhesion events with PETG or silk PLA
damage_avoidance.reason: The failure that actually retires these plates. When a PETG or Bambu PLA Silk footprint bonds harder than the coating adheres to the steel, the part lifts coating away in a patch: instant, localised and permanent. Bambu publishes a PETG-on-SuperTack guide and lists it as supported while forum reports describe exactly this damage, so the risk is disputed in degree rather than in kind and is better prevented than recovered.

damage_avoidance.item: Skipping the nozzle wipe, and wear in the wiping zone itself
damage_avoidance.reason: Two sides of the same instruction. Bambu requires repeated nozzle wiping in the plate's dedicated strip before every print and before auto-levelling, because a bead of cooled filament corrupts the bed-mesh probe and drags through the first layer. The cost is that the wiping strip is where repeated metal-on-coating contact abrades the layer earliest; that is expected consumable behaviour rather than misuse, but it is the first place to watch for wear.

Not addressed by Bambu, and flagged here on substrate grounds. Sodium hypochlorite attacks the chromium oxide passive layer that protects stainless and spring steel, producing pitting and rust that is not reversible by cleaning. On a plate that is a 0.4 mm steel sheet with a 0.05 mm coating, any pinhole, scratch or cut edge is a route to the metal.

damage_avoidance.item: Plastic scraper marks in the coating
damage_avoidance.reason: Recorded for calibration rather than alarm. Bambu acknowledges the coating is comparatively soft and that scraper scratches are cosmetic and do not affect function. They are still worth minimising, because each one is a place where future first layers behave slightly differently, but a scuffed SuperTack plate is not a failed one.

lifespan_notes: Bambu rates the coating at less than 20% adhesion loss after 300 prints under normal use, which is the only published durability figure and assumes PLA at low bed temperatures. Real wear concentrates in two places: the nozzle-wiping strip, where repeated metal-on-coating contact abrades the layer early, and anywhere a scraper has been used. Over-adhesion events with PETG or silk PLA can lift coating in patches, which is instant, localised and permanent. There is no user recoating option and no refinishing service — the plate is a consumable replaced whole, which the roughly USD 15-18 price makes tolerable relative to PEI sheets.

price.notes: Bambu Lab store lists the 256x256 mm Cool Plate SuperTack at about USD 14.99 on sale against a USD 17.99 list price; the 180x180 mm A1 mini size is lower. Cool Plate SuperTack Pro is priced somewhat higher but the exact figure could not be retrieved (store page returned an access error during research).

additional_notes: Single-sided and magnetically mounted on the X1, P1, A1 and A1 mini beds; the spring-steel substrate is the same class used under Bambu's PEI plates, so flatness is comparable. The naming is a persistent source of confusion: SuperTack replaced the older bare-polycarbonate 'Cool Plate', and a good deal of blog and reseller copy still describes the two interchangeably even though the chemistry, price and material compatibility differ. A 'SuperTack Pro' variant exists with a smoother, glossier finish aimed at the same low-temperature materials; Bambu does not publish how its coating formulation differs from the base plate. The honest summary of this surface is that it is excellent at exactly one job — cool, fast, adhesive-free PLA — and progressively worse the further a material sits from that job.

provenance.conflicts: Bambu does not disclose the coating chemistry, so surface_makeup is descriptive rather than analytical. No maximum surface temperature is published; the 70 degC ceiling recorded here is inferred from the supported PLA/PETG envelope, not from a datasheet. PETG is the sharpest disagreement in the sources: Bambu publishes a dedicated PETG-on-SuperTack guide and lists it as supported, while multiple forum threads report over-adhesion, plate damage and unusable first layers — recorded as usable-with-prep rather than either extreme. ABS, ASA, HIPS, nylon, PC and PP are recorded as avoid by absence from the compatibility list rather than by explicit prohibition (only TPU is explicitly prohibited), so those ratings are inference. PVA/BVOH have no vendor guidance at all. Reseller blogs conflate SuperTack with the discontinued bare-polycarbonate Cool Plate, which contaminates several secondary write-ups. Whether any third-party clone of the coating exists is unverified; no plate-only vendor was found making one. SuperTack Pro pricing and its exact coating difference versus the base plate are unverified.
